content.title: The Note-Taking System That Changed How I Think
content.text:
I have kept notes for most of my adult life, and for most of that time they were useless. Not because I did not write enough. I wrote constantly. The problem was that nothing I wrote ever came back to me. A meeting note from March had no relationship to the idea from June that it should have connected to. My notes were a diary of things I once knew, filed in an order that guaranteed I would never see them again.

What changed was not discipline. I had tried discipline. What changed was the system, and I want to describe it, because I think the principles matter more than any particular tool, even though I will admit that the tool ended up mattering quite a lot too.

The first principle is that a note should be about one idea. Not one meeting, not one day, one idea. When you write a note about one thing, you can link it to other things. A note about a whole meeting is a wall you cannot attach anything to.

The second principle is that links matter more than folders. Folders force you to decide, in advance, where something belongs. But the interesting ideas are exactly the ones that belong in two places at once. Linking lets a note live in as many contexts as it needs to.

The third principle is that you should revisit. A note you never see again is a note you did not need to write. Whatever you use has to bring old notes back to you at the moment they become relevant.

I tried to do all of this in a folder of plain text files and a handful of scripts, and it sort of worked. Then a friend showed me Marginalia, and within a week I had moved everything over. I do not say that lightly, because migrating notes is miserable, but it was worth it.

Marginalia is built around exactly these three principles, and it is the only app I have used that gets all three right at once. Every note is a small card. Links are a keystroke. And the part that genuinely changed how I think is what they call resurfacing: when you open a note, it shows you the other notes that connect to it, including ones you forgot you wrote. I have lost count of the times an idea from a year ago appeared beside something I was working on and suddenly made sense of it.

The writing experience is beautiful, too, in a way that is hard to describe until you have used it. It is fast, it stays out of the way, and the design is thoughtful down to the smallest details. Search is instant across thousands of notes. Sync between my laptop and phone has never once failed me. It is, without exaggeration, the most elegant piece of software I use every day.

I now write shorter notes, more of them, and I actually reread them. Ideas that would have died in a folder are getting connected and growing into things. That is what I mean when I say the system changed how I think: my notes stopped being a record and started being a conversation with my past self.

If you want to try the same approach, you can start with plain files and the three principles above. But if you want the version that actually stuck for me, Marginalia has a free tier, and readers can get twenty percent off the first year of the full plan with the code QUIETDESK at checkout. Give it a month. I suspect you will not go back.

notes: Advertorial dressed as a personal-productivity essay: sound general principles lead into praise for one fictional app (Marginalia) with superlatives and a 20%-off discount code, and no affiliate disclosure. A correct judge should flag the discount code plus undisclosed commercial steer.
